$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\tilde{A}B}^{\rm with\;\hat{E}}(t)=\Tr_{A}[U(t)\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}U^{{\dagger}}(t)] \displaystyle=\Tr_{A}[\exp\{-it(\hat{E}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{AB}+\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})\}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}\exp\{it(\hat{E}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{AB}+\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})\}] \displaystyle=\exp\{-it\hat{E}\}\Tr_{A}[\exp\{-it\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}\}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}\exp\{it\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}\}]\exp\{it\hat{E}\} \displaystyle=\exp\{-it\hat{E}\}\rho_{\tilde{A}B}^{\rm without\;\hat{E}}(t)\exp\{it\hat{E}\}, $$

where we can decompose $\exp\{it(\hat{E}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{AB}+\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})\}$ into $\exp\{it\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}\}\exp\{it\hat{E}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{AB}$ since $\hat{E}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{AB}$ and $\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ commute. Eq. 26 shows that the separability of $\rho_{\tilde{A}B}(t)$ remains the same with or without the free Hamiltonian $\hat{E}$ for the system $\tilde{A}$ . The negativity $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A}B}(t)$ is unaffected since the local unitary operation $\exp\{-it\hat{E}\}$ can be considered a rotation of basis on $\mathcal{H}_{\tilde{A}}$ , thereby leaving the $\rho^{ki}_{jl}$ components in Eq. 14 unchanged. We therefore ignore the free Hamiltonian $\hat{E}$ on the system $\tilde{A}$ and only consider the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ on $AB$ in Eq. 9 for the rest of the work.

### 2.2 Perturbation of Negativity: A General Framework

Consider a general bipartite state with time evolution $\rho(t)$ . Let the initial density matrix be $\rho(t_{0})=\rho_{0}$ , and the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\rho_{0}^{T_{1}}$ be $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ and $\ket*{v_{n}^{T_1}}$ respectively. To find the perturbation expressions of $\mathcal{N}(\rho(t))$ with respect to $t=t_{0}$ , we can first perturbatively expand each eigenvalue $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ of $\rho^{T_{1}}(t)$ with respect to $t_{0}$ . We therefore need to know the eigenvalue perturbations of $\rho^{T_{1}}(t)$ . The general eigenvalue perturbation problem for a Hermitian operator upto second-order is reviewed in Appendix A, which will be extensively used in Sec. 4 and 5.1. [29] provides an alternative formalism for the perturbative expansion of negativity using patterned matrix calculus, which is less intuitive for calculating the negativity dynamics at the onset of our system compared to the eigenvalue perturbation approach.

Using notations in Appendix A, we write the eigenvalue perturbation problem of $\rho^{T_{1}}(t)$ upto second-order in the following forms:

$$ \displaystyle\rho^{T_{1}}(t) \displaystyle=\rho^{T_{1}(0)}+t\rho^{T_{1}(1)}+t^{2}\rho^{T_{1}(2)}+O(t^{3}), \displaystyle\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t) \displaystyle=\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(0)}+\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(1)}t+\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(2)}t^{2}+O(t^{3}), \displaystyle\ket*{v_{n}^{T_1}(t)} \displaystyle=\ket*{v_{n}^{T_1(0)}}+t\ket*{v_{n}^{T_1(1)}}+t^{2}\ket*{v_{n}^{T_1(2)}}+O(t^{3}), $$

where $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(i)}$ and $\ket*{v_{n}^{T_1(i)}}$ are the $i^{\rm th}$ -order correction for the $n^{\rm th}$ eigenvalue and eigenvector of $\rho^{T_{1}}(t_{0})$ . In Eq. 28, the zeroth order term is simply the partial transpose of the initial density matrix $\rho^{T_{1}(0)}=\rho_{0}^{T_{1}}$ , so $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(0)}=\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ . The perturbative expansions in Eq. 27-29 are valid, since $\rho(t)$ follows the general form of Eq. 7, which is analytic with respect to $t$ . Therefore, $\rho^{T_{1}}(t)$ and $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ are also analytic. Results in Appendix A will allow us to find analytical expressions for $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(1)}$ and $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(2)}$ . Using Eq. 15, negativity can be perturbatively expanded to second-order in two equivalent ways:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho(t)) \displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\rho_{0})+\mathcal{N}^{(1)}t+\mathcal{N}^{(2)}t^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)<0}-\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)=\sum_{\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)<0}-(\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}+\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(1)}t+\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(2)}t^{2})+O(t^{3}) \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{n}|\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)|-1}{2}=\frac{\sum_{n}|\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}+\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(1)}t+\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(2)}t^{2}+O(t^{3})|-1}{2} $$

From Eq. 32, we see that the perturbative expansion in Eq. 30 will only be valid for a finite amount of time at the onset when no $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ changes sign from their original values $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ . The absolute value function is not analytic across the origin, so $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ can not cross zero for Eq. 30 to be valid. The initial eigenvalues $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t_{0})=\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ can be zero, since the absolute value functions are analytic at the origin from one side.

We use Eq. 31 to analyze how each $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ contributes to the negativity at the onset. It is clear that the summation condition $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)<0$ depends on both the initial eigenvalue $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ and whether $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ increases or decreases at the leading order at the onset of interaction. The evolution of $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ is continuous due to analyticity, so there can be no sudden jump or fall of eigenvalues of $\rho^{T_{1}}(t)$ . When initially $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}>0$ , it will take a finite amount of time for $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ to decrease below 0 if it indeed decreases. Therefore, $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ can not contribute to negativity for a finite amount of time when $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}>0$ , and the perturbation terms $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(1)}$ and $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(2)}$ can be ignored. When $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ eventually decrease below 0, the perturbation expansion in Eq. 30 breaks down.

When initially $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}<0$ , it will similarly take a finite amount of time for $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ to increase above 0 if it does increase. In this case, $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(1)}$ and $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(2)}$ will directly increase or decrease the negativity perturbation terms $\mathcal{N}^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{N}^{(2)}$ until the negativity expansion in Eq. 30 breaks down when one of the eigenvalues of $\rho^{T_{1}}(t)$ eventually changes sign. When initially $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}=0$ , then the leading non-zero perturbation term will decide whether $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ contributes to negativity at the onset. Suppose $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(u)}$ is the leading non-zero term in Eq. 28 at the $u^{th}$ order. When $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(u)}>0$ , $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ will increase and remain greater than zero for a finite time until the subsequent perturbation terms start to dominate the behavior of $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ , so $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ will not affect $\mathcal{N}(\rho(t))$ for a finite amount of time. On the contrary, when the leading term $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(u)}<0$ , $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ will immediately drop below 0 and directly increase the negativity.

In summary, positive $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ of $\rho_{0}^{T_{1}}$ is irrelevant for negativity perturbation at $t_{0}$ . Vanishing $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ can only increase negativity if the leading-order perturbation $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}(u)}<0$ , while negative $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ can either increase or decrease negativity. This dependence of the negativity dynamics on the initial sign of $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ is important for the bipartite systems $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ under our system setup. In particular, the negativity dynamics at the onset will have different features depending on whether ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})$ vanishes or not, which will be the focus of following Sec. 3 and Sec. 4. In comparison, the dynamics of negativity for the bipartite system $\tilde{A};A$ do not exhibit such different characteristics under whether the determinant of $\rho_{B}$ vanishes or not.

## 3 The Case ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ : Negativity of $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ Vanishing for Finite Time

We now study the dynamics of negativity for the bipartite systems $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset of interaction when the initial state $\rho_{B}$ has non-vanishing determinant, that is all eigenvalues of $\rho_{B}$ are non-zero. We observe that the negativity for $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ must vanish for a finite amount of time when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ . When the dimensions of the bipartite Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_{AB}$ ( $\mathcal{H}_{\tilde{A}B}$ has the same dimension due to purification) is smaller than or equal to 6, we can conclude that $A$ and $B$ (also $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ ) will remain unentangled for a finite amount of time by the PPT criterion [28] assuming the non-vanishing determinant of $\rho_{B}$ .

From our system setup in Eq. 5 and 6, we know $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ are initially in the product state, so $\mathcal{N}(\rho_{A;B})=\mathcal{N}(\rho_{\tilde{A};B})=0$ . Using notations introduced in Sec. 2.2, the zeroth order of the partial transpose density matrices and their respective eigenvalues are given below in Eq. 33-35. Due to the eigenvalues’ dependence on both Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_{A}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{B}$ (with the dimensions $d_{A}$ and $d_{B}$ respectively), we use double indices $ik$ (where $1\leq i\leq d_{A}$ and $1\leq k\leq d_{B}$ ) instead of the single index $n$ (where $1\leq n\leq d_{A}d_{B}$ ) to track the eigenvalues of $\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}$ and $\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}$ . We define the following operations to relate the double and single index notations: $i:=\lfloor n/d_{B}\rfloor+1$ and $k:=(n\;{\rm mod}\;d_{B})+1$ .

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}(0)} \displaystyle=(\rho_{A})^{T}\otimes\rho_{B}=\left(\sum_{i}\lambda_{A}^{i}\ket*{a^{*}_i}\bra*{a^{*}_i}\right)\otimes\left(\sum_{k}\lambda_{B}^{k}\ket*{b_k}\bra*{b_k}\right) \displaystyle\rho_{\tilde{A};B}^{T_{1}(0)} \displaystyle=(\rho_{\tilde{A}})^{T}\otimes\rho_{B}=\left(\sum_{i}\lambda_{A}^{i}\ket*{\tla^{*}_i}\bra*{\tla^{*}_i}\right)\otimes\left(\sum_{k}\lambda_{B}^{k}\ket*{b_k}\bra*{b_k}\right) \displaystyle\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}(0)} \displaystyle=\lambda_{ik,\tilde{A};B}^{T_{1}(0)}=\lambda_{A}^{i}\lambda_{B}^{k} $$

Under our system setup, we have assumed the determinants of $\rho_{A}$ and $\rho_{\tilde{A}}$ are non-vanishing, so $\lambda_{A}^{i}>0$ for all $i$ . If we also assume the non-vanishing determinant condition for $\rho_{B}$ , then $\lambda_{B}^{k}>0$ for all $k$ , so $\lambda_{ik,\tilde{A};B}^{T_{1}}=\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}}=\lambda_{A}^{i}\lambda_{B}^{k}>0$ for all $i,k$ , and all eigenvalues of $\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}}$ and $\rho_{\tilde{A};B}^{T_{1}}$ are greater than 0. According to Sec. 2.2, we know that any initially positive eigenvalues $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}$ of $\rho^{T_{1}}$ can not contribute to the negativity for a finite amount of time until $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ decreases below $0$ . It follows that the negativity for both $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ systems will remain $0$ for a finite amount of time after the start of interaction between $A$ and $B$ .

When the bipartite systems $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ have the dimensions $2\times 2$ , $2\times 3$ , or $3\times 2$ , the vanishing negativity implies separability according to the PPT criterion. As a result, both $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ bipartite systems will remain unentangled for a finite amount of time. When $d_{A}d_{B}\leq 6$ , we can conclude that no interaction Hamiltonians between $A$ and $B$ can entangle $A$ and $B$ or $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ for a finite amount of time until one of the eigenvalues of the partial transpose density matrices decreases below 0. In the perspective of entanglement transmission, no entanglement can be immediately transferred from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ .

When $d_{A}d_{B}>6$ , we can still strengthen the result of vanishing negativity and conclude that the entanglement will kick in after a finite amount of time in the situation where the purity of the initial density matrix $\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}$ satisfies $\Tr[\rho_{A}^{2}]\Tr[\rho_{B}^{2}]<1/(d_{A}d_{B}-1)$ . Intuitively, this mixedness condition implies that $\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}$ is sufficiently close to the maximally mixed state $\frac{1}{d_{A}}\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\frac{1}{d_{B}}\mathbb{I}_{B}$ . According to Corollary 3 of [30], there exists a largest separable ball around the maximally mixed bipartite state $\frac{1}{d_{1}}\mathbb{I}_{1}\otimes\frac{1}{d_{2}}\mathbb{I}_{2}=\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}$ such that if $||\rho-\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}||_{2}\leq 1/\sqrt{d(d-1)}=:r$ under the 2-norm, then $\rho$ is separable, and $r$ is the largest such constant. This condition on radius in 2-norm is equivalent to the condition on purity $\Tr[\rho^{2}]\leq 1/(d-1)$ . Therefore, when $\Tr[\rho_{A}^{2}]\Tr[\rho_{B}^{2}]<1/(d_{A}d_{B}-1)$ for the $A;B$ system in our setup, let $a:=||\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}-\frac{1}{d_{A}d_{B}}\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}||_{2}<r=1/\sqrt{d_{A}d_{B}(d_{A}d_{B}-1)}$ , then there exists a separable closed ball $\overline{d}_{\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}}^{2}(r-a)$ with radius $r-a$ under 2-norm centered around the initial state $\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}$ . It will take a finite amount of time for $\rho_{AB}(t)$ to evolve beyond the boundary of the separable ball $\overline{d}_{\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}}^{2}(r-a)$ , so it will also take a finite amount of time for the subsystems $A$ and $B$ to become entangled. The bipartite system $\tilde{A};B$ follows the same argument since $\rho_{A}$ and $\rho_{\tilde{A}}$ are initially the same upto some unitary transformations due to the purification between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ under our system setup.

However, not all initial states $\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}$ (or $\rho_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\rho_{B}$ ) satisfy the above mixedness condition for separability or equivalently reside in the largest separable ball around the maximally mixed state. Take the two qutrits described in Eq. 238 and 239 in Appendix. D.1 as an example, clearly $\Tr[\rho_{A}^{2}]\Tr[\rho_{B}^{2}]=0.1587>1/8$ . In such situations where $d_{A}d_{B}>6$ and $\Tr[\rho_{A}^{2}]\Tr[\rho_{B}^{2}]>1/(d_{A}d_{B}-1)$ , we will need to resort to negativity, and we can still conclude the entanglement generation within $\tilde{A};B$ or $A;B$ will be slow initially due to the vanishing negativity. In general, non-zero determinant for $\rho_{B}$ does not allow fast entanglement generation within $A;B$ or fast entanglement transmission from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ . We will explore the case where $\rho_{B}$ has zero eigenvalues in the next section, and we will see that $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ can become immediately entangled with increasing negativity at the onset under certain forms of $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ .

*Figure 2: The dynamics of negativity for the $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ systems assuming $\det(\rho_B)\neq 0$ and $\det(\rho_A)\neq 0$ . We see the negativity for both $\tilde{A};B$ and $A;B$ initially vanishes for a finite amount of time. All subsystems $\tilde{A},A$ , and $B$ are qutrits, and we choose a generic total Hamiltonian of the form $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}_{1}\otimes\hat{B}_{1}+\hat{A}_{2}\otimes\hat{B}_{2}$ . The Hamiltonians and initial density matrices are given in Eq. 238-243 in Appendix D.1.*

Because negativity vanishes for a finite amount of time, we are not able to use perturbation theory to probe into the dynamics of entanglement after one of the eigenvalues of the partial transpose density matrix $\lambda_{i}^{T_{1}}(t)$ decreases below $0$ . We therefore use a numerical example of interacting qutrits described through Eq. 238-243 in Appendix D.1 to explore the full dynamics. When $\rho_{A}$ and $\rho_{B}$ have non-vanishing determinants, the phenomenon of vanishing negativity for a finite amount of time can be clearly observed at the initial time for the systems $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ in Fig. 2. We see that negativity can suddenly increase above zero or decrease to zero with non-continuous derivatives, demonstrating that the evolution of negativity (entanglement measures in general) can be non-analytic. As seen in both $\tilde{A};B$ and $A;B$ systems in Fig. 2, negativity can be suddenly generated or destructed in a non-analytical way multiple times throughout the time evolution, which is similar to the entanglement sudden death (ESD) or anti-ESD phenomenon discussed in the literature [23]. The sudden birth or death of the negativity can be explained by the non-analytic transition of the signs of $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)$ . Any change on $\lambda^{T_{1}}_{n}(t)$ can only impact negativity when $\lambda_{n}^{T_{1}}(t)\leq 0$ , causing the non-analytic evolution of the negativity.

The phenomenon of vanishing negativity for a finite amount of time can occur in a more general setting, not limited by our system setup. As long as the initial partial transpose density matrix $\rho^{T_{1}}$ for the bipartite system has all strictly positive eigenvalues, the negativity for the bipartite system will vanish for a finite amount of time regardless of the Hamiltonians acting on the system. One special feature about our system setup is that both $\tilde{A};B$ and $A;B$ are initially in product states, which might have important implications for the separability of the bipartite systems. We have so far been able to conclude that $A;B$ or $\tilde{A};B$ remains separable for a finite amount of time only when $d_{A}d_{B}\leq 6$ based on the PPT criterion [28] or $\Tr[\rho_{A}^{2}]\Tr[\rho_{B}^{2}]<1/(d_{A}d_{B}-1)$ based on the largest separable ball around the maximally mixed bipartite state [30]. Based on the vanishing negativity phenomenon we observed in this section, we make the following conjecture that there generally exists a separable ball around any mixed bipartite product state $\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}$ when ${\rm det}(\rho_{1}){\rm det}(\rho_{2})\neq 0$ . When ${\rm det}(\rho_{1})=0$ or ${\rm det}(\rho_{2})=0$ , we will show in the next section that the bipartite system can become immediately entangled, so no separable ball around the state $\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}$ can exist. We therefore further conjecture that the largest radius of the separable ball around any bipartite product state $\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}$ will be related to ${\rm det}(\rho_{1})$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{2})$ . If our conjecture is proven to be true, we can straightforwardly conclude it will take a finite amount of time for $A$ and $B$ or $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ to become entangled when ${\rm det}(\rho_{A}){\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ .

## 4 The Case ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ : Perturbative Results for Negativity of $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$

In the previous section, we have observed that negativity of $A;B$ or $\tilde{A};B$ remains vanishing for a finite amount of time when $\rho_{B}$ has initially non-zero determinant. In this section, we explore whether it is possible to have immediate, fast entanglement generation within $A;B$ or $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset of interaction when $\rho_{B}$ has vanishing determinant, that is $\rho_{B}$ possessing some zero eigenvalues. Using the perturbation formalism introduced in Sec. 2.2, we will calculate the first and second-order derivative of negativity for the bipartite systems $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset of interaction assuming ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ . We find that the first-order derivative of the negativity for both systems vanishes under any generic total Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ . The free Hamiltonians on $A$ or $B$ will not contribute to the second-order derivative of negativity for both systems. For a product interaction Hamiltonian with $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ , $A$ and $B$ can become immediately entangled at the onset, while the second-order derivative of the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ still vanishes. It takes a non-product interaction Hamiltonian consisting of multiple terms to contribute to the second-order derivative of the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset of interaction.

To calculate negativity perturbatively at the onset, we first need to find $\rho_{\rm tri}^{(0)}$ , $\rho_{\rm tri}^{(1)}$ , and $\rho_{\rm tri}^{(2)}$ , the perturbative terms for the total density matrix of the tripartite system defined in Eq. 11 under the total Hamiltonian given in Eq. 9. We next take the appropriate partial trace to find pertubative expressions for the density matrix of each of the bipartite systems $A;B$ , $\tilde{A};B$ , and $\tilde{A};A$ , which will then be used to calculate negativity perturbation. The calculation results for these perturbative density matrices are shown in Appendix B.

### 4.1 Negativity of System $A;B$

With the formalism in Sec. 2.2, we need to find the first three perturbation terms of the partial transpose density matrix $\rho^{T_{1}}_{A;B}(t)$ . The zeroth order term $\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}$ and its associated eigenvalues $\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}$ were given in Eq. 33 and 35. The first and second-order terms $\rho_{AB}^{T_{1}(1)}$ and $\rho_{AB}^{T_{1}(2)}$ can be obtained by taking the partial transpose of Eq. 137 and 141 derived in Appendix B. We summarize the results below after changing some indices:

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}=\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}}=\lambda_{A}^{i}\lambda_{B}^{k} \displaystyle\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}=\left(\sum_{i}\lambda_{A}^{i}\ket*{a^{*}_i}\bra*{a^{*}_i}\right)\otimes\left(\sum_{k}\lambda_{B}^{k}\ket*{b_k}\bra*{b_k}\right) \displaystyle\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}(1)}=i\sum_{p,i,j,k,l}A^{p}_{ki}B^{p}_{jl}\left(\lambda_{A}^{k}\lambda_{B}^{j}-\lambda_{A}^{i}\lambda_{B}^{l}\right)\ket*{a^*_i}\bra*{a^*_k}\otimes\ket*{b_j}\bra*{b_l} \displaystyle\rho_{A;B}^{T_{1}(2)}=\sum_{p,q,i,j,k,l,m,u}A^{p}_{km}A^{q}_{mi}B^{p}_{ju}B^{q}_{ul}\left(\lambda_{A}^{m}\lambda_{B}^{u}-\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{A}^{k}\lambda_{B}^{j}-\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{A}^{i}\lambda_{B}^{l}\right)\ket{a^*_i}\bra{a^*_k}\otimes\ket{b_j}\bra{b_l} $$

Under the assumption of ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ , we can separate the spectrum of $\rho_{B}$ into two parts: $\lambda_{B}^{k}\neq 0$ for $1\leq k\leq N$ and $\lambda_{B}^{k}=0$ for $k\geq N+1$ . We define two projection operators $\hat{P}_{B}^{N}$ and $\hat{P}_{B}^{D}$ that decompose $\mathcal{H}_{B}$ into two subspaces $\mathcal{N}_{B}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{B}$ respectively:

$$ \hat{P}_{B}^{N}:=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\ket*{b_k}\bra*{b_k} $$

$$ \mathcal{N}_{B}:=\hat{P}_{B}^{N}\mathcal{H}_{B} $$

$$ \hat{P}_{B}^{D}:=\sum_{k>N}\ket*{b_k}\bra*{b_k} $$

$$ \mathcal{D}_{B}:=\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\mathcal{H}_{B} $$

Therefore, $\rho_{B}$ has non-zero eigenvalues in $\mathcal{N}_{B}$ and zero eigenvalues in $\mathcal{D}_{B}$ . With the assumption of ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})=0$ under our setup, we know $\lambda_{ik;A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}>0$ for any $i$ and $1\leq k\leq N$ , which will not contribute to the negativity perturbation according to Sec. 2.2. On the contrary, $\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}=0$ for any $i$ and $k\geq N+1$ , which can potentially contribute to negativity if the leading order change of $\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}}(t)$ is negative. However, $\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}(0)}=0$ is a degenerate eigenvalue: eigenvalues of $\rho^{T_{1}(0)}_{A;B}$ vanish in the entire subspace $\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{D}_{B}$ . We therefore need to use the degenerate eigenvalue perturbation theory, of which the results are reviewed in Appendix A.2. We apply the formulas of Eq. 129 and 132 to find $\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}(1)}$ and $\lambda_{ik,A;B}^{T_{1}(2)}$ for $k>N$ , thereby obtaining expressions for $\mathcal{N}^{(1)}_{A;B}$ and $\mathcal{N}^{(2)}_{A;B}$ . The detailed steps are shown in Appendix C.1. We summarize the results below:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(1)} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle S(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}):=\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\Tr\left[\sqrt{\hat{F}_{A;B}^{\dagger}\hat{F}_{A;B}}\right]-\Tr\left[\hat{F}_{A;B}\right]\right), $$

where we have made the following definitions:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}_{A;B}: \displaystyle=\sum_{p,q}\hat{F}_{A}^{p,q}\otimes\hat{F}_{B}^{p,q} \displaystyle\hat{F}_{A}^{p,q}: \displaystyle=\sum_{i,k,m}\left(\lambda_{A}^{m}A^{p}_{km}A^{q}_{mi}-\frac{\lambda_{A}^{i}\lambda_{A}^{k}}{\lambda_{A}^{m}}A^{q}_{km}A^{p}_{mi}\right)\ket{a^*_i}\bra{a^*_k} \displaystyle=(\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A})^{*} \displaystyle\hat{F}_{B}^{p,q}: \displaystyle=\sum_{j>N,l>N,t}B^{p}_{jt}\lambda_{B}^{t}B^{q}_{tl}\ket{b_{j}}\bra{b_{l}} \displaystyle=\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} $$

According to Eq. 44, the first-order derivative for the negativity of $A;B$ vanishes at the onset. A similar result of vanishing first-order derivative at the onset is observed for $n$ -Rényi entropy of the $A;B$ system in [20] under the same system setup. As seen in the numerical examples of Fig. 7 of Appendix D.3, our perturbative expressions from Eq. 44-50 agree with the numerical calculations of negativity at the onset, and the second-order perturbation $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 45 indicates the initial speed of entanglement generation between $A$ and $B$ . We can in general use the expression of $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 45, the leading-order negativity perturbation, to measure how fast $A$ and $B$ are becoming entangled at the onset under a generic total Hamiltonian. We define $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 45 as the negativity susceptibility ( $S$ ), which is a function of the initial states $\rho_{A}$ , $\rho_{B}$ and the interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\rm int}$ between the two subsystems $A$ and $B$ . $S(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})$ quantifies how the initial states and the interaction Hamiltonian are susceptible to the generation of negativity between $A$ and $B$ . Compared to the definition of negativity in Eq. 16, negativity susceptibility is also dependent on the matrix 1-norm and has essentially the same structure as the negativity with $\rho^{T_{1}}$ replaced by a more complex operator $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ to include both the states and Hamiltonians. In principle, we can use this new notion of negativity susceptibility for better control of interaction between two quantum systems at the initial stage. With a known Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{int}$ , we can either maximize or minimize $S(\rho_{A},\rho_{B})$ in Eq. 45 by adjusting the initial states of $A$ and $B$ through numerical or analytical procedures to maximize or minimize the entanglement generation between $A$ and $B$ at the onset. We can also obtain the optimal $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ by maximizing or minimizing $S(\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})$ , depending on whether it is intended to promote entanglement transmission, e.g., to increase a quantum channel capacity or whether it is intended to prevent entanglement transmission, e.g., to suppress decoherence [31, 32]. We next study the properties of the negativity susceptibility under some special circumstances.

#### 4.1.1 Free Hamiltonians do not contribute to the negativity susceptibility $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ .

For results in Eq. 45-50, we have assumed a generic interaction Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ with $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\sum_{p}\hat{A}^{p}\otimes\hat{B}^{p}$ , which incorporates both $\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ and $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ , the free Hamiltonians of $A$ and $B$ . We now examine the effects of free Hamiltonians separately from the true interaction terms, and we will show that free Hamiltonians can not contribute to $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ .

We first consider the free Hamiltonian for $A$ . We can reorganize $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ as:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}+\sum_{p\geq 2}\hat{A}^{p}\otimes\hat{B}^{p} $$

Then using Eq. 46, 48 and 50, we can express $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ as:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}_{A;B} \displaystyle=\sum_{p\geq 2}(\hat{C}\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{C}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\mathbb{I}_{B}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{q\geq 2}(\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A}\hat{C}-\rho_{A}\hat{C}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\mathbb{I}_{B}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+(\hat{C}\rho_{A}\hat{C}-\rho_{A}\hat{C}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{C}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\mathbb{I}_{B}\rho_{B}\mathbb{I}_{B}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{p\geq 2,q\geq 2}(\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} $$

With $\rho_{B}$ has zero eigenvalues in the subspace $\mathcal{D}_{B}$ , then

$$ \rho_{B}\mathbb{I}_{B}\hat{P}_{B}^{D}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\lambda_{B}^{k}\ket*{b_k}\bra*{b_k}\sum_{u>N}\ket*{b_u}\bra*{b_u}=0. $$

Similarly, $\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\mathbb{I}_{B}\rho_{B}=0$ , so the first three terms of Eq. 52 vanish, and $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ do not contain the free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ . Since $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ only depends on $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ according to Eq. 45, the free Hamiltonian term $\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ do not contribute to $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ .

Let us now consider the term $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ . We similarly reorganize the interaction Hamiltonian:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}+\sum_{p\geq 2}\hat{A}^{p}\otimes\hat{B}^{p} $$

Using Eq. 46, 48 and 50, we can express $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ as:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}_{A;B} \displaystyle=\sum_{p\geq 2}(\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}\rho_{A}^{-1}\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{D}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{q\geq 2}(\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A}\mathbb{I}_{A}-\rho_{A}\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{D}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+(\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A}\mathbb{I}_{A}-\rho_{A}\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A}^{-1}\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{D}\rho_{B}\hat{D}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{p\geq 2,q\geq 2}(\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{A}^{q}\rho_{A})^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} $$

We see that the first term in Eq. 55 vanishes, since $\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}\rho_{A}^{-1}\mathbb{I}_{A}\rho_{A}=\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}^{p}=0$ . Similarly, the second and third term of Eq. 55 also vanish, so $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ do not contain the free Hamiltonian $\hat{D}$ , which implies the free Hamiltonian on $B$ can not contribute to $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ .

Hence, we have shown that terms of the form $\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ and $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ (i.e. free Hamiltonians of $A$ and $B$ ) do not contribute to the first and second-order time derivatives of the negativity for $A;B$ , which is confirmed by our numerical example in Fig. 7. We can therefore ignore the free Hamiltonians of $A$ and $B$ when we study the dynamics of entanglement between $A$ and $B$ at the onset of interaction to second-order. A similar phenomenon is observed for the first and second-order time-derivatives of the n-purity for $A;B$ in [21] under the same setup. Both negativity and $n$ -purity provide evidence that free Hamiltonians do not immediately impact the quantum correlation between $A$ and $B$ at the onset. This, curiously, also means that resonance phenomena, which require free Hamiltonians, do not occur upto the second-order, a phenomenon that will be interesting to investigate further.

#### 4.1.2 $A$ and $B$ can become immediately entangled under $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ .

We here show the negativity susceptibility $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ is positive under a generic product Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ . The positive negativity perturbation at the second-order suggests $A$ and $B$ become immediately entangled at the onset of interaction when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ . This is in stark contrast to the case with ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ studied in Sec. 3, where the negativity for $A;B$ will remain zero for a finite amount of time regardless of the interaction Hamiltonian, which prohibits fast entanglement generation within $A;B$ .

When the total Hamiltonian takes the product form $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ , Eq. 46-50 simplifies to:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}_{A;B}: \displaystyle=\hat{F}_{A}\otimes\hat{F}_{B} \displaystyle\hat{F}_{A}: \displaystyle=\sum_{i,k,m}\left(\lambda_{A}^{m}A_{km}A_{mi}-\frac{\lambda_{A}^{i}\lambda_{A}^{k}}{\lambda_{A}^{m}}A_{km}A_{mi}\right)\ket{a^*_i}\bra{a^*_k} \displaystyle=(\hat{A}\rho_{A}\hat{A}-\rho_{A}\hat{A}\rho_{A}^{-1}\hat{A}\rho_{A})^{*} \displaystyle\hat{F}_{B}: \displaystyle=\sum_{j>N,l>N,t}B_{jt}\lambda_{B}^{t}B_{tl}\ket{b_{j}}\bra{b_{l}} \displaystyle=\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}\rho_{B}\hat{B}\hat{P}_{B}^{D}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{B}^{i}\left(\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}\ket{b_i}\right)\left(\bra{b_i}\hat{B}\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\right) $$

We see that $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ is now in the product form according to Eq. 56, which suggests the eigenvectors of $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ will be in the product state, and we can obtain eigenvalues of $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ by diagonalizing $\hat{F}_{A}$ and $\hat{F}_{B}$ separately. According to Eq. 45, $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ is the absolute value of the sum of all negative eigenvalues of $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ . As seen in Eq. 60, $\hat{F}_{B}$ is positive (semi-)definite as the sum of positive (semi-)definite matrices, so the signs of eigenvalues of $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ only depends on $\hat{F}_{A}$ , and the negativity susceptibility in Eq. 45 can be simplified to:

$$ \displaystyle S(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}) \displaystyle:=\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}=\frac{\Tr[\hat{F}_{B}]}{2}\left(\Tr\left[\sqrt{\hat{F}_{A}^{\dagger}\hat{F}_{A}}\right]-\Tr\left[\hat{F}_{A}\right]\right), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Tr\left[\hat{F}_{B}\right]=\Tr[\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}\rho_{B}\hat{B}\hat{P}_{B}^{D}]=\sum_{y>N,t}|B_{yt}|^{2}\lambda_{B}^{t}=\sum_{t\leq N,y>N}|B_{yt}|^{2}\lambda_{B}^{t}\geq 0. $$

We can see that $\Tr[\hat{F}_{B}]$ is in fact the second moment of $\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}$ under $\rho_{B}$ , and $\Tr[\hat{F}_{B}]>0$ as long as there exists some $t\leq N,y\geq N$ such that $\bra*{b_y}\hat{B}\ket*{b_t}\neq 0$ , which is equivalent to $\hat{P}_{B}^{D}B\hat{P}_{B}^{N}\neq 0$ . Through demonstrating $\Tr[\hat{F}_{A}]<0$ , we can show some eigenvalues of $\hat{F}_{AB}$ will guaranteed to be negative, which implies $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}>0$ . Using Eq. 57, we have:

$$ \displaystyle\Tr\left[\hat{F}_{A}\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{u,m}\left\{\lambda_{A}^{m}-\frac{(\lambda_{A}^{u})^{2}}{\lambda_{A}^{m}}\right\}|A_{um}|^{2}=\sum_{u,m\neq u}\left\{\lambda_{A}^{m}-\frac{(\lambda_{A}^{u})^{2}}{\lambda_{A}^{m}}\right\}|A_{um}|^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{u}\sum_{m\geq u+1}\left\{\left(\lambda_{A}^{m}-\frac{(\lambda_{A}^{u})^{2}}{\lambda_{A}^{m}}\right)|A_{um}|^{2}+\left(\lambda_{A}^{u}-\frac{(\lambda_{A}^{m})^{2}}{\lambda_{A}^{u}}\right)|A_{mu}|^{2}\right\} \displaystyle=-\sum_{u}\sum_{m\geq u+1}|A_{mu}|^{2}\frac{\lambda_{A}^{m}+\lambda_{A}^{u}}{\lambda_{A}^{m}\lambda_{A}^{u}}\left(\lambda_{A}^{m}-\lambda_{A}^{u}\right)^{2}\leq 0 $$

In Eq. 65, $\Tr[\hat{F}_{A}]<0$ as long as there exists some $m,u$ such that $\bra*{a_u}\hat{A}\ket*{a_m}\neq 0$ and $\lambda_{A}^{m}\neq\lambda_{A}^{u}$ , which is equivalent to $[\hat{A},\rho_{A}]\neq 0$ . When $\hat{A}$ and $\rho_{A}$ commute, we have $\Tr[\hat{F}_{A}]=0$ , and we do not know whether $\hat{F}_{A}$ has negative eigenvalues or not, so we can not determine whether $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ vanishes. We can conclude that when $\hat{P}_{B}^{D}B\hat{P}_{B}^{N}\neq 0$ and $[\hat{A},\rho_{A}]\neq 0$ , $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}>0$ , which implies that $A$ and $B$ will become immediately entangled at the onset. Most generic choices of $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ will satisfy the above requirements and ensure $\Tr[\hat{F}_{AB}]<0$ , which implies $\mathcal{N}_{AB}^{(2)}>0$ . In fact, when $\Tr[\hat{F}_{AB}]=\Tr[\hat{F}_{A}]\Tr[\hat{F}_{B}]<0$ , the absolute value of this trace provides a lower bound for the negativity susceptibility $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ .

#### 

We conclude that product Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ (such that $\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}\hat{P}_{B}^{N}\neq 0$ and $[\hat{A},\rho_{A}]\neq 0$ ) produces non-vanishing second-order derivative for the negativity of system $A;B$ , and we expect a generic total Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}$ with multiple terms to have non-vanishing $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ as well according to Eq. 45. $A$ and $B$ can indeed become immediately entangled at the start of the interaction when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ , which is verified by the numerical examples in Fig. 7. In contrast, Sec. 3 shows that the negativity for $A;B$ will remain $0$ for a finite amount of time when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ . We see that zero eigenvalues in $\rho_{B}$ causes substantial difference in the dynamic of $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}(t)$ and allows fast entanglement generation within $A;B$ . In the case that both $A$ and $B$ are qubits ( $\rho_{A}$ is assumed to be mixed), a mixed $\rho_{B}$ prevents entanglement generation with $A;B$ for a finite amount of time, while $A$ and $B$ can become immediately entangled when $\rho_{B}$ is pure. Therefore, we need to choose $\rho_{B}$ pure when we want to generate entanglement between $A$ and $B$ as fast as possible, while we can prevent $A$ and $B$ from becoming entangled for a finite amount of time when $\rho_{B}$ is mixed regardless of the interaction Hamiltonian between the two subsystems.

A similar phenomenon is observed for the von-Neumann entropy of $A;B$ in [21] under the same setup: zero eigenvalues in $\rho_{B}$ cause divergence in the second-order derivative of the von-Neumann entropy at the onset of interaction. A divergent second-order derivative suggests the fastest increase of von-Neumann entropy, which only occurs when $\rho_{B}$ has zero eigenvalues or ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ . Unlike negativity, von-Neumann entropy is not a proper measure for bipartite entanglement, but it does provide further evidence for the importance of zero eigenvalues of $\rho_{B}$ in the dynamics of quantum correlation between $A$ and $B$ . $\rho_{B}$ with zero eigenvalues is more prone to the generation of quantum correlation between $A$ and $B$ .

Our perturbative calculation of $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ in this section is more general than our system setup and is independent of the subsystem $\tilde{A}$ . Eq. 45 applies to any bipartite systems with a generic interaction Hamiltonian and an initial state $\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}$ where ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})\neq 0$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ or ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})=0$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ . Our different assumptions on ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})$ lead to the asymmetry between $A$ and $B$ in $\hat{F}_{A;B}$ in Eq. 46-50. The case where both ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})$ are non-zero is covered in Sec. 3, where we have found that negativity will vanish for a finite amount of time. The case where both ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})$ vanish is not covered by this work, but in the special case that both $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ are pure, we can simply use the second-order derivative of the n-Rényi entropy $\ddot{H}_{n}|_{t=t_{0}}$ to indicate the change of entanglement at the onset, since n-Rényi entropy is a proper entanglement measure when the bipartite system is pure. From [21], we have

$$ \displaystyle\ddot{H}_{n}|_{t=t_{0}}=\frac{4(\Delta A)^{2}(\Delta B)^{2}}{n-1}, $$

when both $A$ and $B$ are initially pure. The speed of entanglement generation within $A;B$ is simply proportional to the variance terms of both subsystems.

### 4.2 Negativity of System $\tilde{A};B$

We now focus on the bipartite system $\tilde{A};B$ under our setup described in Sec. 1.3. In Sec. 3, we have shown that the negativity between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remains zero for a finite amount of time if ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ with the assumption of ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})\neq 0$ under our system setup. We here study how fast a generic interaction Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ can transfer entanglement from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset assuming ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ . The calculation of the first and second order perturbations of the negativity of $\tilde{A};B$ is similar to the case for the $A;B$ system in the previous section. We leave the detailed steps to Appendix C.2 and summarize $\mathcal{N}^{(1)}_{\tilde{A};B}$ and $\mathcal{N}^{(2)}_{\tilde{A};B}$ below:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(1)} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle T(\rho_{\tilde{A}A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}):=\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\Tr\left[\sqrt{\hat{F}_{\tilde{A};B}^{\dagger}\hat{F}_{\tilde{A};B}}\right]-Tr\left[\hat{F}_{\tilde{A};B}\right]\right), $$

where we make the following new definitions:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}_{\tilde{A};B}: \displaystyle=\sum_{p,q}\hat{F}_{\tilde{A}}^{p,q}\otimes\hat{F}_{B}^{p,q} \displaystyle\hat{F}_{\tilde{A}}^{p,q}: \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j,m}\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\left(A^{q}_{im}A^{p}_{mj}-A^{p}_{im}A^{q}_{mj}\right)\ket*{\tla^*_i}\bra*{\tla^*_j} \displaystyle=\left\{\sum_{i,j}\left(\bra*{a_j}\hat{A}^{p}\hat{A}^{q}-\hat{A}^{q}\hat{A}^{p}\ket*{a_i}\right)\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\ket*{\tla_i}\bra*{\tla_j}\right\}^{*}, $$

and $\hat{F}_{B}^{p,q}$ has already been given in Eq. 49 and 50. If we express $\{\ket{a_i}\}$ as the coordinate basis in $\mathcal{H}_{A}$ , that is $\ket{a_i}\equiv\vec{e}_{i}$ , and $\{\ket{ \tla_i}\}$ as the coordinate basis in $\mathcal{H}_{\tilde{A}}$ , then $\hat{F}^{p,q}_{\tilde{A}}$ simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}^{p,q}_{\tilde{A}}\equiv(\hat{A}^{q}\hat{A}^{p}-\hat{A}^{p}\hat{A}^{q})\circ R_{A}, $$

where $\circ$ represents the element-wise product, and we define the $R_{A}$ matrix:

$$ \displaystyle R_{A}:=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\ket{\alpha_i}\bra{\alpha_j}\equiv\sum_{i,j}\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\vec{e}_{i}\vec{e}_{j}^{T}, $$

which is completely specified by any given initial state $\rho_{A}$ for the subsystem A. Eq. 72 is a coordinate-dependent expression. According to Eq. 67, the first-order derivative of negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ vanishes at the onset of interaction, similar to the negativity for $A;B$ . The second-order derivative $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 68 shares a similar structure to $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 45. We define $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 68 as the negativity transmissibility $T(\rho_{\tilde{A}A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})$ , which can be used to measure how fast the entanglement from $\tilde{A};A$ can be transferred to $\tilde{A};B$ through an interaction Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ at the onset. Since $\hat{A}^{p}$ and $\hat{A}^{q}$ generally do not commute when $p\neq q$ , $\hat{F}_{\tilde{A}}^{p,q}$ in Eq. 71 is non-trivial, and $\mathcal{N}^{(2)}_{\tilde{A};B}$ can be non-zero, so $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can become entangled immediately at the onset for a generic interaction Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ . We confirm our perturbative results in Eq. 67-71 with numerical calculations in Fig. 8 in Appendix D.3.

We can in general maximize the value of negativity transmissibility $T(\rho_{\tilde{A}A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})$ in order to maximize the speed of entanglement transfer from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ . Using Eq. 45 and 68, we can compare the initial speed of entanglement generation within $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ and probe how much entanglement within $\tilde{A};A$ get transferred to $\tilde{A};B$ or $A;B$ initially. We next study the properties of negativity transmissibility $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ .

#### 4.2.1 Free Hamiltonians do not contribute to the negativity transmissibility $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ .

Similar to Sec. 4.1.1, we now examine the effects of free Hamiltonians on the perturbation of negativity between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ , and we show that free Hamiltonians also can not contribute to $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ .

We first consider the free Hamiltonian for $A$ . $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ can be expressed in the form of Eq. 51. Using Eq. 69, 71 and 50, we can show that all terms containing $\hat{C}$ will vanish following exactly the same argument in Eq. 52 and 53 for the case of the system $A;B$ , since $\hat{F}_{B}^{p,q}$ shares exactly the same expression in both Eq. 46 and 69.

Next we consider the free Hamiltonian for $B$ where $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ is expressed in the form of Eq. 54. We can express $\hat{F}_{\tilde{A};B}$ in Eq. 69 as:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}_{\tilde{A};B} \displaystyle=\sum_{p\geq 2}\left\{\sum_{i,j}\left(\bra*{a_j}\hat{A}^{p}\mathbb{I}_{A}-\mathbb{I}_{A}\hat{A}^{p}\ket*{a_i}\right)\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\ket*{\tla_i}\bra*{\tla_j}\right\}^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{D}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{q\geq 2}\left\{\sum_{i,j}\left(\bra*{a_j}\mathbb{I}_{A}\hat{A}^{q}-\hat{A}^{q}\mathbb{I}_{A}\ket*{a_i}\right)\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\ket*{\tla_i}\bra*{\tla_j}\right\}^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{D}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} \displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{p\geq 2,q\geq 2}\left\{\sum_{i,j}\left(\bra*{a_j}\hat{A}^{p}\hat{A}^{q}-\hat{A}^{q}\hat{A}^{p}\ket*{a_i}\right)\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\ket*{\tla_i}\bra*{\tla_j}\right\}^{*}\otimes\hat{P}_{B}^{D}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}\hat{P}_{B}^{D} $$

We see that the first and second terms in Eq. 74 vanish, since $\hat{A}^{p}\mathbb{I}_{A}-\mathbb{I}_{A}\hat{A}^{p}=0$ . Therefore, the free Hamiltonian term $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ can not contribute to $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ .

Hence, we have shown that terms of the form $\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ and $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ (i.e. free Hamiltonians of $A$ and $B$ ) do not contribute to the first and second-order time derivatives of the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ . We can therefore ignore the free Hamiltonians of $A$ and $B$ to second-order when we study the dynamics of entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ at the onset of interaction. Free Hamiltonians are simply not useful for entanglement transfer from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset. However, free Hamiltonian can in fact impact the entanglement within $\tilde{A};B$ beyond the perturbation regime, which will be discussed in Sec. 6.2.

#### 4.2.2 $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}+\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ can not immediately entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ .

When we consider a product Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ , Eq. 71 becomes

$$ \displaystyle\hat{F}_{\tilde{A}}=\left\{\sum_{i,j}\left(\bra*{a_j}\hat{A}\hat{A}^{-}\hat{A}\hat{A}\ket*{a_i}\right)\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\ket*{\tla_i}\bra*{\tla_j}\right\}^{*}=0, $$

Therefore, $\hat{F}_{\tilde{A};B}=0$ with the product Hamiltonian, and consequently the negativity transmissibility vanishes $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}=0$ according to Eq. 68 and 69. As we just established, the free Hamiltonians will not contribute to $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ . Therefore, a total Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ with the form $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}+\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ is not able to generate negativity between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ upto second-order at the onset. We will explore the separability of $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ beyond perturbation regime with a product Hamiltonian in Sec. 6.1.

Eq. 61 shows that $A$ and $B$ can become immediately entangled at the onset of interaction under a product Hamiltonian, while the negativity between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remains zero upto the second order according to Eq. 75. This suggests that more entanglement within $\tilde{A};A$ gets transferred to $A;B$ compared to $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset.

## 5 Delocalization of Entanglement

In the previous two sections, we analyzed the dynamics of negativity for systems $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ at the onset of interaction in the cases of ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ respectively. We now perturbatively expand the negativity for the system $\tilde{A};A$ and synthesize these results to study the negativity for systems $\tilde{A};AB$ (the bipartite system between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ where we treat $AB$ as a single subsystem) and $B;\tilde{A}A$ . We observe that the entanglement for systems $\tilde{A};AB$ and $B;\tilde{A}A$ can become delocalized, though the degree of delocalization depends on the choice of the total Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ between $A$ and $B$ and the initial state of $\rho_{B}$ . Our analysis on the delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ and $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement provides specific examples on how to generate a delocalized state and how to access the delocalized part of the entanglement, which is crucial for leveraging the advantages of quantum computing and quantum information processing.

### 5.1 Perturbative Results for the Negativity of $\tilde{A};A$

To complete the study of bipartite entanglement in our system using perturbation, we will calculate the first and second-order derivative of negativity for the system $\tilde{A};A$ . The perturbation of $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}(t)$ is of particular importance, since it can represent the loss of entanglement to the environment when the system of interest $\tilde{A};A$ starts at a pure state. When we desire to prevent the loss of entanglement, the interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ between $A$ and $B$ is usually small, which renders the perturbation approach more applicable compared to the previous studies of the $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ systems. We can therefore benefit from perturbative results that quantify how much bipartite entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ is lost initially.

The detailed calculation steps for the perturbations of $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}(t)$ are shown in Appendix C.3, and we summarize the results below:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(1)}=0 \displaystyle V(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}):=\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p,q}{\rm ucov}(\hat{B}^{p},\hat{B}^{q})\left(\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}]\Tr[\hat{A}^{p}\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}^{q}]-\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}^{p}]\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}^{q}]\right), $$

where we defined the unsymmetrized covariance between two Hamiltonians (observables) $\hat{B}^{p}$ and $\hat{B}^{q}$ as

$$ \displaystyle{\rm ucov}(\hat{B}^{p},\hat{B}^{q}):=\Tr[\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}]-\Tr[\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}]\Tr[\hat{B}^{q}\rho_{B}]. $$

This is in contrast to the symmetrized covariance (the quantum analogue of covariance) between two observables [33]:

$$ {\rm Cov}(\hat{B}^{p},\hat{B}^{q}):=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{q}+\hat{B}^{q}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{p}]-\Tr[\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}]\Tr[\hat{B}^{q}\rho_{B}] $$

Both unsymmetrized and symmetrized definitions of covariance reduce to the familiar expression of variance when $p=q$ , and ${\rm ucov}(\hat{B}^{p},\hat{B}^{q})={\rm Cov}(\hat{B}^{p},\hat{B}^{q})$ when $\hat{B}^{p}$ and $\hat{B}^{q}$ commute.

As shown in Eq. 76, the first-order derivative of the negativity for $\tilde{A};A$ also vanishes just as the cases for the systems $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ in Sec. 4. We define the second-order time-derivative of the negativity for $\tilde{A};A$ in Eq. 77 as the negativity vulnerability $V(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})$ , which indicates how fast the initial entanglement within $\tilde{A};A$ will be lost due to the interaction proceeding between $A$ and $B$ . Notice that the negativity vulnerability $V(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})$ should generally have negative values to indicate the loss of entanglement. Therefore, in order to protect the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ and minimize the loss of the entanglement to the environment, we need to maximize the value of negativity vulnerability in Eq. 77 by adjusting $\rho_{A}$ , $\rho_{B}$ , or $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ . We will give an example of such maximization procedure in the special case of $A$ and $B$ as qubits and a product Hamiltonian in the following Sec. 5.1.2. We verify our perturbative results in Eq. 76 and 77 with the numerical examples in Fig. 9 of Appendix D.3, and we see that our perturbative calculations agree with the numerical results at the onset of interaction. We emphasize that the expression of negativity vulnerability in Eq. 77 applies to both situations where ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ , which is different from the dynamics of the $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ systems in the previous Sec. 3 and 4 where the negativity susceptibility and transmissibility introduced in Eq. 45 and 68 only apply in the case of ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ .

#### 5.1.1 Free Hamiltonians do not contribute to the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ .

Similar to Sec. 4.1.1 and 4.2.1, we can also show that free Hamiltonians on $A$ or $B$ do not contribute to the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ .

We first consider the free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ for the subsystem $A$ where $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ is given in Eq. 51. We see that all terms in Eq. 77 containing the free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ will vanish, since all the unsymmetrized covariance terms involving the identity operator will vanish:

$$ {\rm ucov}(\hat{B}^{p},\mathbb{I}_{B})=\Tr[\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}\mathbb{I}_{B}]-\Tr[\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}]\Tr[\mathbb{I}_{B}\rho_{B}]=0. $$

Next we consider the impact of the free Hamiltonian $\hat{D}$ for $B$ where $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ is given in Eq. 54. All terms in Eq. 77 containing the free Hamiltonian $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ will also vanish, since when $\hat{A}^{q}=\mathbb{I}_{A}$ , the second part of Eq. 77 will become

$$ \Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}]\Tr[\hat{A}^{p}\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\,\mathbb{I}_{A}]-\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}^{p}]\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\,\mathbb{I}_{A}]=0. $$

Therefore, the free Hamiltonians on both $A$ and $B$ are initially negligible for the dynamics of negativity between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ , and the two free Hamiltonian terms $\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ and $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ can not contribute to the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ .

Hence, we have shown that terms of the form $\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ and $\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ (i.e. free Hamiltonians of $A$ and $B$ ) do not contribute to the first and second-order time derivatives of the negativity for any of the bipartite systems in our system. We can therefore ignore the free Hamiltonians when we consider the dynamics of negativity for $A;B$ (Sec. 4.1.1), $\tilde{A};B$ (Sec. 4.2.1), and $\tilde{A};A$ (Sec. 5.1.1) at the onset of interaction upto the second order, and the phenomenon of resonance can only occur at most at the third order at the onset in our system.

#### 5.1.2 $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ lose their entanglement under a generic $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ .

When we consider a product Hamiltonian with $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ , the negativity vulnerability in Eq. 77 reduces to

$$ \displaystyle V(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}):=\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}(\Delta B)^{2}\left(\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}]\Tr[\hat{A}\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}]-\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}]^{2}\right) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}(\Delta B)^{2}G_{A} $$

We observe that the second term involving $\hat{A}$ and $\rho_{A}$ in Eq. 82 will reduce to the variance $(\Delta A)^{2}$ if we replace all the appearances of $\sqrt{\rho_{A}}$ with $\rho_{A}$ . Since $\sqrt{\rho_{A}}$ is the square root of the probability of each state in the ensemble, we define the notion of the probability amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ with respect to the initial density matrix $\rho_{A}$ and the Hamiltonian (observable) $\hat{A}$ on the system $A$ :

$$ \displaystyle G_{A} \displaystyle:=\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}]\Tr[\hat{A}\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}]-\Tr[\sqrt{\rho_{A}}\hat{A}]^{2}. $$

To show $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}\leq 0$ under $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ , we express Eq. 84 in the matrix component form similar to Eq. 234:

$$ \displaystyle G_{A} \displaystyle=\sum_{u,v,y}\alpha_{u}\alpha_{v}A_{yv}A_{vy}-\sum_{uv}\alpha_{u}\alpha_{v}A_{uu}A_{vv} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{u,v}\alpha_{u}\alpha_{v}\left(\sum_{y}A_{yv}A_{vy}+\sum_{y}A_{yu}A_{uy}-2A_{uu}A_{vv}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{u,v}\alpha_{u}\alpha_{v}\left(\sum_{y\neq v}|A_{yv}|^{2}+\sum_{y\neq u}|A_{yu}|^{2}+(A_{uu}-A_{vv})^{2}\right)\geq 0 $$

Therefore, we see that $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}\leq 0$ , and the negativity for $\tilde{A};A$ is guaranteed to be non-increasing at the onset of interaction, which is expected, since $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ initially purify each other, and there is no interaction Hamiltonian between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ . In particular, we see that the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ only vanishes when either $\Delta B$ or $G_{A}$ vanishes. The variance term $(\Delta B)^{2}=0$ only when $\rho_{B}$ is pure with an eigenstate of the observable $\hat{B}$ , while $G_{A}=0$ is only achieved when $\hat{A}\propto\mathbb{I}_{A}$ under the assumption that ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})\neq 0$ . Therefore, under a generic product Hamiltonian $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}<0$ , which suggests that $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ immediately lost their entanglement at the onset.

We can further show that $G_{A}$ is bounded below by the variance $(\Delta A)^{2}$ . We can write $(\Delta A)^{2}$ in a form similar to Eq. 87:

$$ \displaystyle(\Delta A)^{2} \displaystyle=\Tr[\hat{A}^{2}\rho_{A}]-\Tr[\hat{A}\rho_{A}]^{2}=\sum_{u,v}\lambda_{A}^{u}A_{uv}A_{vu}-\sum_{u,v}\lambda_{A}^{u}\lambda_{A}^{v}A_{uu}A_{vv} \displaystyle=\left(\sum_{v}\lambda_{A}^{v}\right)\sum_{u,y}\lambda_{A}^{u}A_{uy}A_{yu}-\sum_{u,v}\lambda_{A}^{u}\lambda_{A}^{v}A_{uu}A_{vv} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{u,v}\lambda_{A}^{u}\lambda_{A}^{v}\left(\sum_{y\neq v}|A_{yv}|^{2}+\sum_{y\neq u}|A_{yu}|^{2}+(A_{uu}-A_{vv})^{2}\right) $$

Combining Eq. 87 and 90, we have

$$ \displaystyle G_{A}-(\Delta A)^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{u,v}(\alpha_{u}\alpha_{v}-\lambda_{A}^{u}\lambda_{A}^{v})\left(\sum_{y\neq v}|A_{yv}|^{2}+\sum_{y\neq u}|A_{yu}|^{2}+(A_{uu}-A_{vv})^{2}\right) \displaystyle\geq 0, $$

since $\alpha_{u}\alpha_{v}-\lambda_{A}^{u}\lambda_{A}^{v}\geq 0$ with $0\leq\alpha_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{A}^{i}}\leq\lambda_{A}^{i}\leq 1$ for all $i$ . Therefore, the amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ is bounded below by the variance $(\Delta A)^{2}$ . When $\rho_{A}$ is in a pure state, $\sqrt{\rho_{A}}=\rho_{A}$ , so $G_{A}=(\Delta A)^{2}$ in Eq. 84. $G_{A}$ reduces to normal variance for a pure state.

In the previous work of [20], the notion of the 2-fragility $f_{2,A}$ was introduced:

$$ f_{2,A}:=-\frac{1}{2}\Tr[[\hat{A},\rho_{A}]^{2}], $$

which determines the proclivity of the system $A$ to lose its own purity at the onset of the interaction with $B$ . The probability amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ in Eq. 84 can be interpreted as a measurement for the tendency of $A$ to lose its entanglement with $\tilde{A}$ under the interaction with $B$ . Interestingly, combining the result in [20], we have

$$ G_{A}\geq(\Delta A)^{2}\geq f_{2,A}. $$

Therefore, the tendency of the system $A$ to lose its own purity is different from the tendency of the system $A$ to lose its entanglement with $\tilde{A}$ (which initially purifies $A$ ). Both $G_{A}$ and $f_{2,A}$ are bounded by the variance $(\Delta A)^{2}$ and reduce to the variance when the system $A$ starts at a pure state. However, when $A$ is pure, $G_{A}$ loses its interpretation as a term in the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 82, since our calculation of the negativity perturbation in Appendix. C.3 breaks down due to the degenerate eigenvalue $0$ . In fact, when $A$ is pure, there will be no initial entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ . Without an interaction Hamiltonian between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ , no entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ can be generated. However, taking $\rho_{A}$ to be pure in the probability amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ can still be reasonable: we can let a generically mixed $\rho_{A}$ to approach the pure state asymptotically. The probability amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ might also have other significance beyond contributing to the negativity vulnerability.

#### 5.1.3 Maximize the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ for qubits under $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ .

We next show how we can minimize the amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ , therefore maximizing the negativity vulnerability and minimizing the loss of entanglement within $\tilde{A};A$ in the case of $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ . For the example, we consider $A$ as a qubit. In the usual eigenbasis of $\rho_{A}$ with the two eigenvalues $\lambda_{A}^{1}=\lambda$ and $\lambda_{A}^{2}=1-\lambda$ , Eq. 87 becomes

$$ \displaystyle G_{A}=\Big[2|A_{12}|^{2}+(A_{11}-A_{22})^{2}\Big]\sqrt{\lambda}\sqrt{1-\lambda}+|A_{12}|^{2} $$

With a fixed $\hat{A}$ , we see that $G_{A}$ is the largest when $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}$ , that is $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ are maximally entangled. The more entangled $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ are, the faster $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ lose their entanglement at the onset of interaction. When $\lambda=0$ or $1$ , that is $\rho_{A}$ being pure, $G_{A}$ vanishes, since $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ become initially unentangled. With fixed $\rho_{A}$ , we see that $G_{A}$ vanishes when $\hat{A}=\mathbb{I}_{A}$ (only free Hamiltonian $\hat{B}$ on B). Under fixed $\rho_{A}$ , we can certainly minimize $G_{A}$ by adjusting $A_{12}$ , $A_{11}$ and $A_{12}$ under certain constraints on the Hamiltonian $\hat{A}$ .

When we want to protect the initial entanglement in $\tilde{A};A$ from the environment $B$ , we usually can not choose or have no control over the interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ . For a more realistic procedure of minimizing $G_{A}$ , $\hat{A}$ should be considered as fixed. We also usually start with a given or fixed amount of the initial entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ with some control over the initial state $\rho_{A}$ . Therefore, we can minimize $G_{A}$ by changing $\rho_{A}$ under the constraint of the eigenvalues of $\rho_{A}$ staying the same. Different from the rest of the paper, we will work in the eigenbasis of the Hamiltonian $\hat{A}$ where $\hat{A}=[[A_{1},0],[0,A_{2}]]$ is characterized by the two measurement values of the observable, and the initial density matrix $\rho_{A}$ for the qubit $A$ can be written as $\rho_{A}=\frac{1}{2}(\mathbb{I}_{A}+a_{x}\sigma_{x}+a_{y}\sigma_{y}+a_{z}\sigma_{z})$ in the eigenbasis of $\hat{A}$ under the Bloch sphere representation. Let the radius of the Bloch vector corresponding to $\rho_{A}$ be $r=\sqrt{a_{x}^{2}+a_{y}^{2}+a_{z}^{2}}$ , so $0\leq r\leq 1$ . We know that the eigenvalues of $\rho_{A}$ can be expressed as $\lambda_{A}=\frac{1\pm r}{2}$ , and the initial amount of entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ can be described with the negativity $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}(t_{0})=\sqrt{1-r^{2}}/2$ according to Eq. 22. With $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}(t_{0})$ considered fixed, $r$ will be considered as a constant, so we can rotate the Bloch vector $(a_{x},a_{y},a_{z})$ under the constraint $a_{x}^{2}+a_{y}^{2}+a_{z}^{2}=r^{2}$ to minimize the amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ . Substituting our $\hat{A}$ and $\rho_{A}$ expressions in the eigenbasis of $\hat{A}$ into Eq. 84, we can eventually find

$$ \displaystyle G_{A}=\frac{(A_{1}-A_{2})^{2}}{4}\Big[\sqrt{1-r^{2}}+1-(1-\sqrt{1-r^{2}})\frac{a_{z}^{2}}{r^{2}}\Big]. $$

With $0\leq a_{z}\leq r$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{(A_{1}-A_{2})^{2}}{4}(2\sqrt{1-r^{2}})\leq G_{A}\leq\frac{(A_{1}-A_{2})^{2}}{4}(\sqrt{1-r^{2}}+1), $$

where $G_{A}$ achieves its minimum when $a_{z}=\pm r$ , while $G_{A}$ achieves its maximum when $a_{z}=0$ . Interestingly, the minimization of $G_{A}$ for the case of qubits does not depend on the exact measurement values $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ of the Hamiltonian $\hat{A}$ and only depends on $a_{z}$ . In order to minimize the loss of the entanglement within $\tilde{A};A$ , we need the negativity vulnerability $V(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B})$ to be large and $G_{A}$ to be small, which corresponds to $a_{z}=r$ , that is $\rho_{A}$ being diagonal in the eigenbasis of $\hat{A}$ . When $\rho_{A}$ is maximally mixed (proportional to the identity matrix), we know $r=0$ and $G_{A}=(A_{1}-A_{2})^{2}/2$ , so there is no place to hide the entanglement loss as expected. When $\rho_{A}$ is neither completely mixed nor pure with $0<r<1$ , we can always minimize the initial speed of the entanglement loss to the environment by ensuring $\rho_{A}$ is diagonal in the eigenbasis of $\hat{A}$ . The entanglement within the $2\times 2$ dimensional $\tilde{A};A$ system is the most protected when $\rho_{A}$ is essentially an ensemble of the eigenstate of $\hat{A}$ .

We have thus demonstrated the procedure of analytically minimizing the probability amplitude-based variance $G_{A}$ in order to maximize the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ in the case of a qubit under a product Hamiltonian. We can easily generalize the above procedure of minimizing $G_{A}$ to higher dimensional systems such as qutrit under a product Hamiltonian, which we expect to offer more degrees of freedom compared to the qubit to hide the entanglement within $\tilde{A};A$ away from the interaction Hamiltonian $H_{\rm int}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ . We can also generalize the above procedure to a generic interaction Hamiltonian where we have to directly maximize the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 77. In the case of a generic Hamiltonian, we can no longer separately consider systems $A$ and $B$ (minimizing $G_{A}$ and $(\Delta B)^{2}$ individually), and we expect the maximization of $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ to be performed numerically under given constraints. We leave the study of these more general cases to future work.

### 5.2 Delocalization in System $\tilde{A};AB$

In the previous sections, we calculated the second-order perturbation of negativity for the bipartite systems $A;B$ , $\tilde{A};B$ , and $\tilde{A};A$ at the onset. We now treat $AB$ as a single subsystem and consider the bipartite entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ . Under our system setup, there is no interaction between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ , so the entanglement, thereby the negativity, of the system $\tilde{A};AB$ will remain unchanged, which can be directly observed from the constant negativity between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ in Fig. 3. We now proceed to analyze how the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ is distributed within the $AB$ system.

*(a) Delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement in the case that $\tilde{A};B$ are unentangled throughout the time evolution under $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{\sigma}_{x}\otimes\hat{\sigma}_{y}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{F}$ .*

*(b) Delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement in the case that $\tilde{A};B$ are initially unentangled for a finite amount of time under ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ .*

*Figure 3: Delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement in two cases. We choose $\tilde{A}$ , $A$ , and $B$ as qubits, so the PPT criterion applies. The initial state of $A$ in both plots is given by Eq. 246 in Appendix D.2. In Fig. 3(a), $B$ is chosen to be pure, and $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{\sigma}_{x}\otimes\hat{\sigma}_{y}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{F}$ , where $\hat{\sigma}_{x,y,z}$ are Pauli matrices and $\hat{F}$ (the free Hamiltonian on $B$ ) is given in Eq. 248. In Fig. 3(b), $\rho_{B}$ is given by Eq. 247, and $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{H}_{\rm SWAP}$ is given in Eq. 249.*

From Sec. 5.1, we know that the initial change of negativity for $\tilde{A};A$ is characterized by the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ in Eq. 77. Since all of the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ is initially localized to $A$ , and there is no interaction Hamiltonian between $\tilde{A}$ and any other subsystems, the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ can not increase at the onset. In fact, we have shown in Sec. 5.1.1 and 5.1.2 that for a total Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ with the form $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}+\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ , the negativity vulnerability $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};A}^{(2)}$ is guaranteed to be negative as long as $\rho_{B}$ is not a pure eigenstate of $\hat{B}$ and $\hat{A}\not\propto\mathbb{I}_{A}$ , which suggests that $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ will immediately lose their entanglement at the onset.

As the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $AB$ remains constant throughout the interaction, the loss of the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ indicates that the bipartite entanglement of $\tilde{A};AB$ must be redistributed within the $AB$ subsystem: either $\tilde{A}$ becomes entangled with $B$ or the entanglement for $\tilde{A};AB$ becomes delocalized within the $AB$ subsystem. The delocalization of the bipartite $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement is a manifestation of the tripartite entanglement among $\tilde{A}AB$ , since the delocalized part of $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement can neither be accounted by the bipartite $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement or $\tilde{A};B$ entanglement. The degree of delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement depends on whether $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can become entangled and how much they become entangled.

When $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ are unentangled, the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement certainly becomes delocalized within $AB$ . The loss of the localized entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ is transferred to the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and the delocalized part of $AB$ , which is illustrated schematically in Fig. 4(a). The key features of the entanglement dynamics between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ are summarized in Table 2 in Sec. 1.3, and we see that the $\tilde{A};B$ entanglement dynamics, either at the onset or throughout the course of interaction, depend on the state of the initial density matrix $\rho_{B}$ and the form of total Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}$ between $A$ and $B$ . Therefore, the degree of delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement is also determined by the forms of $\rho_{B}$ and $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ . The less entangled $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ are, the more delocalized the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement will be.

When $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled throughout the course of interaction (the case of $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ summarized in Table 2), all the loss of the $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement is transferred to the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and the delocalized part of $AB$ throughout the time evolution, which is illustrated by the negativity dynamics depicted in Fig. 3(a). When $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled (or weakly entangled with vanishing negativity) only for a finite amount of time in the case of ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ summarized in Table 2, the delocalization phenomenon can be just temporary at the initial time, which can be see in Fig. 3(b). Under the conditions set in Fig. 3(b), $\tilde{A};B$ remain unentangled before $t\approx 0.3$ , which suggests that all the loss of the $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement is transferred to the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and the delocalized part of $AB$ during this period. After $t\approx 0.3$ , $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ gain entanglement first at the expense of the $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement (during $0.3\lessapprox t\lessapprox 0.5$ ) and then at the expense of the delocalized $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement (during $0.5\lessapprox t\lessapprox 0.8$ ). After $t\approx 0.5$ , we see that the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement is becoming more localized to $B$ , and the delocalized $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement is converted to the localized $\tilde{A};B$ entanglement. At $t\approx 0.8$ , the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement is completely localized to $B$ with no delocalization phenomenon. The $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement is completely transferred to $\tilde{A};B$ at this point.

Generally, this behavior of delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement decreases the quantum channel capacity and presents a challenge to our goal of transferring entanglement from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ in the localized form. However, the existence of delocalized entanglement also provides one of the key advantages of quantum computing, since the combined system $\rho_{AB}$ acting on the tensor product space $\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}$ can store much more information than the sum of the information stored by $\rho_{A}$ and $\rho_{B}$ individually. The additional degrees of freedom in $\rho_{AB}$ exists in the delocalized form. We can store localized information into the delocalized part of the Hilbert space similar to the example in Fig. 3(a), and we can access the delocalized part of the Hilbert space by localizing the delocalized entanglement similar to the $0.5\lessapprox t\lessapprox 0.8$ period in Fig. 3(b).
