### 5.3 Delocalization in System $B;\tilde{A}A$

Similar to the previous Sec. 5.2 where we considered $AB$ as a single subsystem, we can also treat $\tilde{A}A$ as a single subsystem and consider the dynamics of the bipartite entanglement between $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ . The total Hamiltonian between $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ can then be written as $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}^{B;\tilde{A}A}=\sum_{p}\hat{B}^{p}\otimes(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{A}^{p})$ based on Eq. 8 and 9. Under our system setup, $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}$ starts in a pure state.

When ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ , the $B;\tilde{A}A$ system will then reduce to the case studied in Sec. 4.1 with $A$ and $B$ replaced by $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ respectively. Applying results from Eq. 44 to 50, we can find the expressions for the first and second-order perturbation of the negativity between $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ at the onset of interaction:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{B;\tilde{A}A}^{(1)} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{B;\tilde{A}A}^{(2)} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\Tr\left[\sqrt{\hat{F}_{B;\tilde{A}A}^{\dagger}\hat{F}_{B;\tilde{A}A}}\right]-\Tr\left[\hat{F}_{B;\tilde{A}A}\right]\right) \displaystyle\hat{F}_{B;\tilde{A}A}: \displaystyle=\sum_{p,q}\Big(\hat{B}^{q}\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{p}-\rho_{B}\hat{B}^{p}\rho_{B}^{-1}\hat{B}^{q}\rho_{B}\Big)^{*}\otimes\Big(\hat{P}_{\tilde{A}A}^{D}(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{A}^{p})\rho_{\tilde{A}A}(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{A}^{q})\hat{P}_{\tilde{A}A}^{D}\Big) \displaystyle\hat{P}_{\tilde{A}A}^{D} \displaystyle=\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}A}-\rho_{\tilde{A}A}, $$

where $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}$ is given in Eq. 1. When the total Hamiltonian between $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ takes the product form $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}^{B;\tilde{A}A}=\hat{B}\otimes(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{A})$ , we know that $\mathcal{N}_{B;\tilde{A}A}^{(2)}>0$ when $[\hat{B},\rho_{B}]\neq 0$ and $(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}A}-\rho_{\tilde{A}A})(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{A})\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\neq 0$ based on the analysis in Sec. 4.1.2, so a generic product Hamiltonian is sufficient to immediately generate entanglement between $B$ an $\tilde{A}A$ at the onset when $\rho_{B}$ is not maximally mixed. We also expect that a generic interaction Hamiltonian containing multiple terms can also immediately entangle $B$ with $\tilde{A}A$ at the onset, which can be seen from the topmost curve in Fig. 5 as an example.

*Figure 5: Delocalization of the $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement under ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ . For $t\lessapprox 0.3$ , the newly generated $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement (transferred from the initial $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement) is completely delocalized as $B$ remain unentangled with both $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ . We here choose $\tilde{A}$ , $A$ , and $B$ as qubits, and the initial states and $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ used here are the same at those for Fig. 3(b) listed in Appendix. D.2.*

When ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ , our perturbative calculations in Sec. 4 no longer apply. With the initial density matrices of both $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ subsystems containing vanishing eigenvalues, the perturbation of negativity becomes more complicated due to the additional structures present in the degenerate eigenspace for the vanishing eigenvalue. However, we still expect $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ to gain entanglement at the onset of interactions under a generic total Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ , since zero eigenvalues are generally prone to entanglement generation. In the special case when $B$ is pure, the total $\tilde{A}AB$ system is pure, so we can use n-Rényi entropy as an entanglement measure for $B;\tilde{A}A$ . The perturbative result for the n-Rényi entropy in Eq. 66 from [20] shows that $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ will become immediately entangled under a generic product Hamiltonian on $AB$ . Therefore, we expect $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ to become entangled under a generic $\rho_{B}$ and $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ .

The generation of entanglement within the bipartition $B;\tilde{A}A$ is in fact an indication for the establishment of genuine tripartite entanglement in the total system $\tilde{A}AB$ , which is equivalent to all three bipartitions $\tilde{A};AB$ , $A;\tilde{A}B$ , and $B;\tilde{A}A$ being bipartitely entangled [34]. The entanglement (negativity) between $\tilde{A};AB$ will remain constant as established in Sec. 5.2, and $B;\tilde{A}A$ (with $\rho_{B}$ pure) will become immediately entangled at the onset under a generic $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ as discussed in this section. The bipartition $A;\tilde{A}B$ is not studied in this work, but since $A$ is initially entangled with $\tilde{A}$ under our setup, we know $A$ and $\tilde{A}B$ are initially entangled. Therefore, the total system $\tilde{A}AB$ will become tripartitely entangled as $B$ become entangled with $\tilde{A}A$ at the onset.

We next proceed to analyze how the entanglement between $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ is distributed within the $\tilde{A}A$ system. In the case of ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ , we know $\mathcal{N}_{A;B}(t)=\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}(t)=0$ for a finite amount of time after the start of interaction between $A$ and $B$ based on Sec. 3. However, we know the negativity for $B;\tilde{A}A$ increases immediately from Eq. 99 under a generic $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}$ , which indicates that most, if not all, of the entanglement generated between $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ exists between $B$ and the delocalized part of $\tilde{A}A$ . In the case of $A$ and $B$ as qubits (dim $(\mathcal{H}_{A})$ dim $(\mathcal{H}_{B})\leq 6$ ), $B$ remain unentangled with both $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ for a finite amount of time while $B$ becomes entangled with $\tilde{A}A$ at the same time, which indicates that the generated $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement is completely delocalized, which is demonstrated in the region with $t\lessapprox 0.3$ in Fig. 5. The existing $\tilde{A}A$ entanglement is transferred to the entanglement between $B$ and the delocalized part of $\tilde{A}A$ . However, such complete delocalization of the $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement is only temporary. We expect $B$ and $A$ to become entangled after a finite amount time ( $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can also become entangled depending on the forms of $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ and $\rho_{B}$ shown in Table. 2), so part of the $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement become localized again after this initial period as seen in the $t\gtrapprox 0.3$ region of Fig. 5. The $t\lessapprox 0.3$ period in Fig. 5 provides an example for generating purely delocalized entanglement.

When ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ , we have shown in Sec. 4.1 that $B$ will become immediately entangled with $A$ under a generic total Hamiltonian for $AB$ and a generic state $\rho_{B}$ , which prevents the existence of the complete delocalization of the $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement under generic cases. However, a complete delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement is still possible for ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ under some special circumstances: we can simply add an ancilla $\tilde{B}$ to purify $B$ in the system described in Fig. 5 such that ${\rm det}(\rho_{\tilde{B}B})=0$ while the $\tilde{B}B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement is still completely delocalized within $\tilde{A}A$ for an initial period.

Combining the analysis in this section and the previous Sec. 5.2, we see that when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ , both delocalization of the $\tilde{A};AB$ entanglement and delocalization of the $B;\tilde{A}A$ entanglement can occur simultaneously for a finite amount of time after the start of interaction between $A$ and $B$ , which is demonstrated by the $t\lessapprox 0.3$ region in Fig. 3(b) and 5 with the same initial states and $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ . The original $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement is transferred to the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and the delocalized part of $AB$ as well as the entanglement between $B$ and the delocalized part of $\tilde{A}A$ . In the case of $A$ and $B$ as qubits, we see that the localized $\tilde{A};A$ entanglement is only transferred to the entanglement in the delocalized form, which provides a mechanism to store information in the delocalized part of the Hilbert space.

## 6 When can an interaction $\hat{H}_{{\rm int}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ transmit entanglement?

In Sec. 3, we see that the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ will vanish for a finite amount of time when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ regardless of the total Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ in $AB$ . In Sec. 4.2, we have established that the negativity transmissibility $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ given in Eq. 68 vanishes at the onset under a total Hamiltonian of the form $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}+\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ between $A$ and $B$ when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ . In this section, we go beyond the perturbative calculation of the $\tilde{A};B$ negativity and study under what forms of $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}$ can the the entanglement within $\tilde{A};A$ be transmitted to $\tilde{A};B$ during the interaction between $A$ and $B$ .

### 6.1 Without Free Hamiltonians: no entanglement transmission

We first consider a product Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{H}_{{\rm int}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ where free Hamiltonians on $A$ and $B$ are ignored. According to Eq. 7, the time evolution is given by

$$ \rho(t)=U(t)\rho_{\rm tri}U^{{\dagger}}(t)=e^{-it(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B})}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}e^{it(\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B})} $$

We express $U(t)$ in the eigenbasis of $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ . Assume $\hat{A}=\sum_{i}h_{A}^{i}\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}$ and $\hat{B}=\sum_{j}h_{B}^{j}\ket*{h_B^j}\bra*{h_B^j}$ , then $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes\ket*{h_B^j}=h_{A}^{i}h_{B}^{j}\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes\ket*{h_B^j}$ , which are the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ . It is important for our proof that the eigenvectors of $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ are in the product form themselves. The unitary operator can then be decomposed in the following form:

$$ \displaystyle U(t) \displaystyle=\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\exp\{-it\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}\}=\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\sum_{i,j}\exp\{-ith_{A}^{i}h_{B}^{j}\}\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}\otimes\ket*{h_B^j}\bra*{h_B^j} \displaystyle=\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\sum_{j}\exp\{-ith_{B}^{j}\hat{A}\}\otimes\ket*{h_B^j}\bra*{h_B^j} \displaystyle=\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\sum_{i}\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}\otimes\exp\{-ith_{A}^{i}\hat{B}\} $$

Using Eq. 102 and 105, we proceed to show $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled throughout the time evolution:

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\tilde{A}B}(t)=\Tr_{A}[\rho(t)]=\Tr_{A}[U(t)\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}U^{{\dagger}}(t)] \displaystyle=\Tr_{A}[\sum_{i}\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}\otimes\exp\{-ith_{A}^{i}\hat{B}\}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}\sum_{j}\ket*{h_A^j}\bra*{h_A^j}\otimes\exp\{ith_{A}^{j}\hat{B}\}] \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\Tr_{A}[\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^j}\bra*{h_A^j}]\otimes\exp\{-ith_{A}^{i}\hat{B}\}\rho_{B}\exp\{ith_{A}^{j}\hat{B}\} \displaystyle=\sum_{e}\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}\otimes\exp\{-ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\}\rho_{B}\exp\{ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\} \displaystyle=\sum_{e}\Tr_{\tilde{A}}[\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}]\frac{\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}}{\Tr_{\tilde{A}}[\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}]}\otimes\exp\{-ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\}\rho_{B}\exp\{ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\} \displaystyle=\sum_{e}\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{A}\ket*{h_A^e}\frac{\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}}{\Tr[\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}]}\otimes\exp\{-ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\}\rho_{B}\exp\{ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\} $$

We analyze each term in Eq. 111. Let $\rho_{\tilde{A}}^{e}:=\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}/\Tr[\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}]$ . $\rho_{\tilde{A}}^{e}$ is clearly a density matrix acting on $\mathcal{H}_{\tilde{A}}$ , since $\rho_{\tilde{A}}^{e}$ is Hermitian and positive-definite with $\Tr[\rho_{\tilde{A}}^{e}]=1$ according to its definition. Let $\rho_{B}^{e}(t):=\exp\{-ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\}\rho_{B}\exp\{ith_{A}^{e}\hat{B}\}$ , which is simply the time evolution of the system $B$ under the new free Hamiltonian $h_{A}^{e}\hat{B}$ , so $\rho_{B}^{e}(t)$ is a density matrix acting on $\mathcal{H}_{B}$ . Last, we define $p_{e}:=\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{A}\ket*{h_A^e}$ , We have $p_{e}\geq 0$ and $\sum_{e}p_{e}=\Tr[\rho_{A}]=1$ where $\rho_{A}$ is the initial density matrix for the system A. We can now write

$$ \rho_{\tilde{A}B}(t)=\sum_{e}p_{e}\rho_{\tilde{A}}^{e}\otimes\rho_{B}^{e}(t), $$

and according to Eq. 12 in Sec. 2.1, we see that $\rho_{\tilde{A}B}(t)$ is separable for any time $t$ , so $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled during the entire time evolution. Therefore, it is impossible to transfer any entanglement from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ with a product Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ .

Notice that the above separability proof from Eq. 106 to 112 is independent of the exact form of the initial density matrices $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}$ and $\rho_{B}$ . Though we assumed that $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ purify each other and ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})\neq 0$ for our system setup, $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ will remain unentangled under the product Hamiltonian regardless of the initial relation between systems $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ as long as the the total system is initially in a product state $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}$ . In fact, the above proof for the separability of $\tilde{A};B$ under a product Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ can be generalized to the situation where $\tilde{A}A$ and $B$ are initially separable (that is $\rho_{\tilde{A}AB}=\sum_{k}q_{k}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}^{k}\otimes\rho_{B}^{k}$ where $\sum_{k}q_{k}=1$ ) by adding an additional summation over all expressions of the proof. The above proof also works when $\tilde{A}$ , $A$ , and $B$ are infinite dimensional systems.

If $B$ is initially entangled with another system $\tilde{B}$ (when $B$ is mixed we can purify $B$ with an ancillary $\tilde{B}$ similar to what we did to $A$ ), then by the symmetry of our system setup, we know that $A$ and $\tilde{B}$ will also remain unentangled during the course of their time evolution if we choose $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ .

#### 6.1.1 Non-zero quantum discord for qubits with $\rho_{B}$ pure under $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ .

Even though $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled throughout the time evolution under $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ for $AB$ , $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can still have quantum correlation in the form of discord [35]. The condition for $D(A,B)=0$ , a vanishing discord between system A and B, is the more restrictive condition (compared to the separability criterion in Eq. 12) that the bipartite state can be written in the form $\rho=\sum_{k}\rho_{1}^{k}\otimes\ket{k}_{2}\bra{k}_{2}$ , where $\{\ket{k}_{2}\}$ is an orthonormal basis for the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ . Clearly, discord is asymmetric, that is generically $D(A,B)\neq D(B,A)$ . Discord is also a resource that could provide a quantum advantage in some cases, albeit smaller than the advantage provided by entanglement [36]. Using results in [37], we will show that $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can possess quantum discord when $\tilde{A},A$ and $B$ are qubits and the initial state $\rho_{B}$ is pure under a product Hamiltonian.

As discussed in Sec. 5.3, the total system $\tilde{A}AB$ will become genuinely tripartitely entangled as $B$ and $\tilde{A}A$ become entangled at the onset under a generic product Hamiltonian on $AB$ . When the initial state $\rho_{B}$ is pure, the total system $\tilde{A}AB$ will remain in a pure state. $\tilde{A};A$ is initially entangled in our system setup, and $A;B$ (with $\rho_{B}$ pure) will become immediately entangled at the onset under a generic $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ as shown in Sec. 4.1.2. For three qubits in a total pure state, [37] showed that the presence of both bipartite and genuine tripartite entanglement in the total system require the presence of discord between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ . In particular, with $A$ entangled with $\tilde{A}$ , $D(\tilde{A},B)>0$ ; and with $A$ become entangled with $B$ , we will have $D(B,\tilde{A})$ become positive.

Therefore, the system $\tilde{A};B$ can have quantum discord even though they remain unentangled under $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ in the case of qubits with $\rho_{B}$ being pure. Quantum discord is indeed easier to generate and transfer compared to entanglement. We can in fact perform analytical calculation to quantify the initial change of discord using perturbation theory or plot the dynamics of discord numerically in the case of three qubits at a total pure state, since the entanglement of formation, which enters the expression of discord, simplifies to concurrence in the $2\times 2$ dimensional system [38]. We can no longer conclude the presence of discord between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ when systems become larger than qubits or the initial state $\rho_{B}$ becomes mixed, which is no longer covered by [37] as discord can no longer be easily calculated analytically. However, we still suspect the presence of quantum discord between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ in the generic case.

### 6.2 With Free Hamiltonians

We next consider the cases where the free Hamiltonian for system $A$ or $B$ becomes non-negligible. Let the free Hamiltonian of $A$ be $\hat{C}$ and the free Hamiltonian of $B$ be $\hat{D}$ . We examine the two cases where $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ or $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ respectively, that is we include either one of the free Hamiltonians for $A$ and $B$ . We show that $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled with the inclusion of only free Hamiltonian $\hat{D}$ for system $B$ , while $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can become entangled when the free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ for system $A$ is included, yet inefficiently at the onset.

#### 6.2.1 The case $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ : no entanglement transmission.

We first consider the case of a product interaction Hamiltonian with a free Hamiltonian for $B$ . Assuming $\hat{A}=\sum_{i}h_{A}^{i}\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}$ and $\hat{B}=\sum_{j}h_{B}^{j}\ket*{h_B^j}\bra*{h_B^j}$ , $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ have eigenvalues $v_{li}$ and eigenvectors of the product form $\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes\ket*{v_{li}}$ , where $\{v_{li}|l\in\mathbb{N}\}$ and $\{\ket*{v_{li}}|l\in\mathbb{N}\}$ are eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the self-adjoint operator $h_{A}^{i}\hat{B}+\hat{D}$ on $\mathcal{H}_{B}$ . Indeed,

$$ \displaystyle(\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D})\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes\ket*{v_{li}} \displaystyle=h_{A}^{i}\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes\hat{B}\ket*{v_{li}}+\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes\hat{D}\ket*{v_{li}} \displaystyle=\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes(h_{A}^{i}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\ket*{v_{li}}=v_{li}\ket*{h_A^i}\otimes\ket*{v_{li}} $$

Eq. 114 yields

$$ \displaystyle U^{{\rm with}\;\hat{D}}(t) \displaystyle=\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\sum_{i,l}\exp\{-itv_{li}\}\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}\otimes\ket*{v_{li}}\bra*{v_{li}} \displaystyle=\mathbb{I}_{\tilde{A}}\otimes\sum_{i}\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}\otimes\exp\{-it(h_{A}^{i}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\} $$

The proof for $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remaining unentangled with the inclusion of $\hat{D}$ for system $B$ is then similar to the case in Eq. 107-111 under Sec. 6.1 by replacing $h_{A}^{i}\hat{B}$ with $h_{A}^{i}\hat{B}+\hat{D}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\tilde{A}B}^{{\rm with}\;\hat{D}}(t) \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\Tr_{A}[\ket*{h_A^i}\bra*{h_A^i}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^j}\bra*{h_A^j}]\otimes \displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\exp\{-it(h_{A}^{i}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\}\rho_{B}\exp\{it(h_{A}^{j}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\} \displaystyle=\sum_{e}\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}\otimes\exp\{-it(h_{A}^{e}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\}\rho_{B}\exp\{it(h_{A}^{e}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\} \displaystyle=\sum_{e}p_{e}\rho_{\tilde{A}}^{e}\otimes\rho_{B}^{e}(t), $$

where we defined $\rho_{\tilde{A}}^{e}:=\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}/\Tr[\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\ket*{h_A^e}]$ , $\rho_{B}^{e}(t):=\exp\{-it(h_{A}^{e}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\}\rho_{B}\exp\{it(h_{A}^{e}\hat{B}+\hat{D})\}$ , and $p_{e}:=\bra*{h_A^e}\rho_{A}\ket*{h_A^e}$ with $\sum_{e}p_{e}=\Tr[\rho_{A}]=1$ . Therefore, we know $\rho_{\tilde{A}B}^{{\rm with}\;\hat{D}}(t)$ remains separable according to Eq. 12. The inclusion of a free Hamiltonian $\hat{D}$ for system $B$ on the product interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ can not entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ . Similar to the previous Sec. 6.1, the above separability proof is also independent of the exact form of the initial density matrices $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}$ and $\rho_{B}$ , and it works for both finite and infinite dimensional systems. Since $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled, the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ vanishes, which is numerically verified in Fig. 6.

*Figure 6: The negativity dynamics for $\tilde{A};B$ under different forms of total Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}$ between $A$ and $B$ in our system setup. We choose both $A$ and $B$ as qutrits with $\rho_{A}$ given in Eq. 238 and $\rho_{B}$ assumed to be pure. The Hamiltonians listed in the legend are chosen as Eq. 240-245 in Appendix D.1. We see that the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ vanish for a product-form interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ with or without a free Hamiltonian $\hat{D}$ on $B$ , while the addition of a free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ on $A$ can entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ . A generic interaction Hamiltonian of multiple terms can also entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ .*

#### 6.2.2 The case $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ : entanglement can be transmitted.

In the special case when $\hat{C}$ commutes with $\hat{A}$ , we can factor the unitary operator $\hat{U}(t)$ into products, and $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain unentangled:

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\tilde{A}B}(t)=\Tr_{A}[\exp\{-it(\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B})\}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\otimes\rho_{B}\exp\{it(\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B})\}] \displaystyle=\Tr_{A}\left[\exp\{-it\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}\}\Big(\exp\{-it\hat{C}\}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\exp\{it\hat{C}\}\Big)\otimes\rho_{B}\exp{it\hat{A}\ot\hat{B}}\right] \displaystyle=\Tr_{A}\left[\exp\{-it\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}\}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}^{\hat{C}}(t)\otimes\rho_{B}\exp{it\hat{A}\ot\hat{B}}\right], $$

where we defined $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}^{\hat{C}}(t)=\exp\{-it\hat{C}\}\rho_{\tilde{A}A}\exp\{it\hat{C}\}$ . We can then show that $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ are separable by replacing $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}$ with $\rho_{\tilde{A}A}^{\hat{C}}(t)$ in the proof of Eq. 106-111 in Sec. 6.1.

With a generic free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ which does not commute with $\hat{A}$ , the proof strategy for separability used in Sec. 6.1 and 6.2.1 break down. $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can indeed become entangled, which is proved by the numerical example illustrated through the blue (solid) curve of Fig. 6. Therefore, the total Hamiltonian of the form $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ can entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ , while $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ can not. In this sense, the free Hamiltonian on $A$ is more useful than the free Hamiltonian on $B$ for the entanglement transfer from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ . The case for $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ with the inclusion of both free Hamiltonians is similar to the case of $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ : $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ remain separable when $[\hat{A},\hat{C}]=0$ , while they can become entangled when $[\hat{A},\hat{C}]\neq 0$ , which is demonstrated by the numerical example corresponding to the purple (dash-dot) curve in Fig. 6.

Even though the inclusion of the free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ on $A$ to the product interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ can entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ during the time evolution, such entanglement transfer from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ will be slow initially, characterized by the vanishing first and second derivatives of the negativity between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ at the onset. Both blue (solid) and purple (dash-dot) curves in Fig. 6 show this feature of slow negativity generation at the onset. When ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ , the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ vanishes for a finite amount of time as discussed in Sec. 3, which guarantees that all orders of derivatives of $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}(t)$ will vanish at the onset. When ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ , we showed in Sec. 4.2 that the first and the second order perturbations $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}^{(2)}$ (corresponding to the first and second derivatives of $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}(t)$ at the onset) vanish when the total Hamiltonian can be written in the form of $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{A}\otimes{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}+\mathbb{I}_{A}\otimes\hat{D}$ . Therefore, the transfer of entanglement from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ will be slow at the onset even when we consider the free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ for $A$ in addition to the product interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{{\rm int}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ .

### 6.3 Interactions with multiple terms: efficient transmission of entanglement.

When the interaction Hamiltonian between $A$ and $B$ contains multiple terms where $\hat{H}_{{\rm int}}=\sum_{p}\hat{A}^{p}\otimes\hat{B}^{p}$ , we showed in Sec. 4 that $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ will generically become entangled to the second-order at the onset when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ , and we can characterize the rate of the entanglement generation with the negativity transmissibility introduced in Eq. 68. We therefore expect a generic interaction Hamiltonian with multiple terms to be able to transfer the entanglement from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ during the time evolution.

The green (middle) curve in Fig. 5 and the black (topmost) curve in Fig. 6 give examples of $\hat{H}_{{\rm int}}=\sum_{p}\hat{A}^{p}\otimes\hat{B}^{p}$ entangling $\tilde{A};B$ in the cases of ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ and ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ respectively. As discussed in Sec. 3 and 4, ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ allows fast entanglement generation at the onset, while ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})\neq 0$ forces $\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{A};B}(t)$ to vanish for a finite amount of time initially. Notice that in the case of Fig. 5 where $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{H}_{\rm SWAP}=\hat{\sigma_{x}}\otimes\hat{\sigma_{x}}+\hat{\sigma_{y}}\otimes\hat{\sigma_{y}}+\hat{\sigma_{z}}\otimes\hat{\sigma_{z}}$ , even though $\hat{\sigma_{x}}\otimes\hat{\sigma_{x}}$ , $\hat{\sigma_{y}}\otimes\hat{\sigma_{y}}$ , and $\hat{\sigma_{z}}\otimes\hat{\sigma_{z}}$ commute with each other, that is the individual terms of $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}$ commute with each other, $\hat{H}_{\rm SWAP}$ can still entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ . This suggests $\hat{H}_{\rm tot}$ can entangle $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ even if all the individual Hamiltonian terms commute with each other.

From the previous 6.2.2, $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}+\hat{C}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{B}$ allows entanglement transfer from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ , but the negativity for $\tilde{A};B$ initially vanishes upto the second order, thereby rendering the transmission slow. In comparison, the interaction Hamiltonian of multiple terms can transmit entanglement immediately at the second order when ${\rm det}(\rho_{B})=0$ . Therefore, when we want fast entanglement transfer from $\tilde{A};A$ to $\tilde{A};B$ , we should always use a generic interaction Hamiltonian containing multiple terms, and the negativity transmissibility in Eq. 68 provides guidance on how to maximize the speed of the entanglement transfer. When we want to minimize the initial speed of the entanglement transmission, we should adopt a product-form interaction Hamiltonian. If we want to avoid the entanglement between $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ altogether, we should choose specific interaction Hamiltonians $\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ where $\hat{A}$ dominates the free Hamiltonian $\hat{C}$ of $A$ such that $\hat{C}$ can be neglected.

## 7 Conclusions and Outlook

Due to entanglement, the state of a composite quantum system $\tilde{A}A$ can and generally does contain delocalized quantum information. The question arises, therefore, how the efficiency with which entanglement can be transmitted from system to system in an interaction depends on the Hamiltonians and states involved. This question is of foundational interest when applied to the fundamental interactions in nature. At the same time, this question is of practical interest for quantum technologies, for example, for the purpose of constructing large quantum processors from smaller modules. To this end, in order to access the full tensor product Hilbert space of the collection of modules, entanglement will need to be efficiently transmitted and spread across the modules.

To study a prototypical scenario for the transmission of entanglement, we considered the situation in which a system $A$ is initially entangled with and purified by an ancilla $\tilde{A}$ , i.e., where $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ initially share delocalized quantum information. We then let $A$ interact with a system $B$ . During the interaction, system $\tilde{A}$ keeps constant entanglement with the combined system $AB$ . At the same time, system $\tilde{A}$ can lose entanglement with $A$ and gain entanglement with $B$ , i.e., entanglement with $\tilde{A}$ can be transmitted from $A$ to $B$ . We analyzed the dynamics of this entanglement transfer and we also found that systems $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ can become discorded before they become entangled. This behavior is related to the fact that discord is a remnant of tri-partite entanglement after one of three subsystems, here $A$ , is traced over, see [37].

Our focus, however, has been on the dynamics of entanglement transfer. To this end, we quantified magnitudes of entanglement by using the entanglement monotone negativity. We worked with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and we obtained both nonperturbative and perturbative results, as summarized in Table 1 and 2.

For the perturbative results, we expanded to the second order in time, i.e., we studied the dynamics of the transfer of entanglement at the onset of the interaction between systems $A$ and $B$ . We did not expand in coupling constants, i.e., we do allow strong couplings, which is useful since strong couplings can occur in quantum technologies [39, 40]. We found, for example, the perturbative result that free Hamiltonians do not affect the change of negativity at the onset of an interaction, up to the second-order in time, which is consistent with our prior findings regarding the evolution of coherent information [20, 21]. Further, we saw that the free Hamiltonian of $\tilde{A}$ never impacts the entanglement transfer (see Eq. 26 in Sec. 2.1).

Considering possible interaction Hamiltonians, we saw, for example, that, to second order in time, interaction Hamiltonians of the simple form $H_{\rm int}=\hat{A}\otimes\hat{B}$ cannot transfer entanglement regardless of the free Hamiltonians of the systems $\tilde{A}$ , $A$ and $B$ . In fact, such interaction Hamiltonians will leave $\tilde{A}$ and $B$ unentangled throughout the entire time evolution - if or as long as the free Hamiltonian of $A$ can be neglected.

More generally, we analyzed how arbitrary interaction Hamiltonians and arbitrary initial states influence the proclivity of an interaction to either generate, transfer or lose entanglement. We found that these three proclivities are captured by three quantities that are Hamiltonian and state dependent and that we call negativity susceptibility (Eq. 45), negativity transmissibility (Eq. 68), and negativity vulnerability (Eq. 77), respectively.

For example, the notion of negativity transmissibility quantifies the efficiency of the transfer of entanglement at the onset of an interaction. The use of this measure may help experimental efforts to either prevent entanglement transfer (e.g., to prevent decoherence), or to optimize entanglement transfer, e.g., for quantum communication. For example, interaction Hamiltonians and/or the use of suitable regions in state space could be engineered so as to extremize the negativity transmissibility. The negativity transmissibility could also serve as all or part of the cost function for the training of a neural network, e.g., for the purpose of machine-learned quantum error correction or error prevention [41, 42, 43].

For another example, the negativity vulnerability can be useful to identify those subsystems of the Hilbert space of $A$ , in which entanglement with $\tilde{A}$ is relatively safe from decoherence and, conversely, to identify subsystems in which entanglement with $\tilde{A}$ is at an elevated risk of decohering. We note here that since a subsystem can be specified by giving the observables of the subsystem, it should be possible to describe entanglement vulnerability not only in terms of subsystems but also in terms of observables. This then suggests a connection to the study of entanglement dynamics in the Heisenberg picture [44, 45, 46, 47], which should depend on both the initial states and the observables (interaction Hamiltonians), similar to the notion of the negativity susceptibility $S(\rho_{A},\rho_{B},\hat{H}_{{\rm tot}})$ in Eq. 45.

While our results here have been derived under the assumption that the Hilbert spaces involved are finite dimensional, it will also be very interesting to generalize these results to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. What we can say so far, is, for example, that our calculations for the negativity susceptibility and negativity transmissibility for the $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ systems in Sec. 4 still hold if $B$ is infinite dimensional, under the condition that $\rho_{B}$ possesses only a finite number of non-zero eigenvalues and $\tilde{A}$ and $A$ remain finite dimensional.

This means that, in principle, it is possible to apply our results to a system consisting of two atoms, $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ , and a quantum field, $B$ , as long as the field’s initial density matrix is of finite rank and as long as we take into account only finitely many energy levels of the atoms. For practical applications, the situation is somewhat subtle because a careful UV cutoff would generally be necessary. This is because, in practice one might expect the field to be in a state with a thermal background. On one hand, the condition that $\rho_{B}$ possesses finite rank would then be violated. On the other hand, it could be argued that for the field to violate the finite rank condition, the field would, unrealistically, have to thermalize infinitely far into the ultraviolet (i.e., e.g., even beyond the Planck scale).

Our perturbative calculation for the negativity of the $\tilde{A};A$ system in Sec. 5.1 is more general. The notion of negativity vulnerability (Eq. 77) applies to any situation where $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ are finite dimensional while $B$ can be infinite dimensional without restrictions. In particular, the notion of negativity vulnerability for the $\tilde{A};A$ system can also be applied if $B$ is in a thermal state (while negativity susceptibility (Eq. 45) and negativity transmissibility (Eq. 68) for the $A;B$ and $\tilde{A};B$ systems do not straightforwardly apply if $B$ is in a thermal state).

Also, our calculations have assumed that $A$ is finite dimensional and that ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})\neq 0$ . It will be very interesting to generalize our perturbative results to the case with ${\rm det}(\rho_{A})=0$ and, finally, for the case in which $\tilde{A},A$ and $B$ are allowed to be infinite dimensional systems. For a related paper on the question what genuinely new phenomena may arise for infinite-dimensional systems, see, e.g., [46].
